title: Between the Testaments
summary: From Nehemiah to Jesus: the last of Persian rule, Alexander, the Ptolemies and Seleucids, the persecution under Antiochus IV, the Maccabean revolt, the Hasmonean kingdom, Rome and Herod, the Apocrypha, and what these centuries gave the New Testament world.

sections.h: Four hundred years that were not silent
sections.body:
Turn the page from Malachi to Matthew in a Protestant Bible and more than four centuries pass without a word. The last events of the Old Testament, Nehemiah's second term as governor of Judah, fall around 430 BC; Malachi probably prophesied about the same time. When Matthew opens, Judea is ruled by a king named Herod under the authority of Rome, the Jews speak Aramaic and Greek, synagogues stand in every town, Pharisees and Sadducees argue in the temple courts, and many are waiting for a Messiah. Nothing in the Old Testament explains how that world came to be. The period between is sometimes called ‘the four hundred silent years’, because no prophet of the canon spoke in it, but it was one of the most eventful periods in Jewish history.

The main sources are the books of 1 and 2 Maccabees, which cover the crisis of the 160s BC and its aftermath; the Jewish historian Josephus, whose Jewish Antiquities (about AD 93 or 94) retells the whole period; Greek and Roman historians such as Polybius; the Dead Sea Scrolls, discovered from 1947 onward; and a large body of Jewish writings from these centuries. Some of those writings, the books Catholic and Orthodox Christians call deuterocanonical and Protestants call the Apocrypha, are included in some Bibles and not others, as the last section of this guide explains. The book of Daniel, whatever one concludes about its date, speaks at length about these centuries in the form of visions, and the Old Testament's final prophetic words point forward across them: “Behold, I will send My messenger, who will prepare the way before Me.” (Malachi 3:1).

The story falls into five periods: the last century of Persian rule (to 332 BC); the Greek conquest and the rule of the Ptolemies of Egypt (332 to about 200); the rule of the Seleucids of Syria, ending in persecution (about 200 to 167); the Maccabean revolt and the independent Hasmonean state (167 to 63); and Roman rule through Herod the Great (63 to 4 BC).

sections.body:
The Old Testament closes with Judah as a small temple community in the Persian province of Yehud, perhaps no more than a few tens of thousands of people around Jerusalem. After Nehemiah, Persian governors ruled beside the high priests, and the high priest became the leading figure of Jewish life, a role he kept until the Maccabees. Aramaic, the administrative language of the Persian Empire, became the everyday language of Jews in the land; by the first century Hebrew was used mostly for Scripture and learning, and the synagogue readings needed Aramaic paraphrases, the Targums.

This period saw a lasting division between Jews and Samaritans. The people of the old northern territory around Samaria, descended from Israelites who had remained and from the peoples the Assyrians resettled there (2 Kings 17:24-41), worshiped the LORD but were rebuffed when they offered to help rebuild the temple in Jerusalem (Ezra 4:1-3). They built their own temple on Mount Gerizim, above Shechem. Josephus dates it to Alexander's time, but excavations directed by Yitzhak Magen from 1983 to 2003 found that the sacred precinct was first built in the fifth century BC, in the Persian period. The Samaritans kept the five books of Moses, in their own edition, the Samaritan Pentateuch, as their Scripture. By Jesus' day the hostility was deep: “Jews do not associate with Samaritans” (John 4:9).

Many Jews never returned from exile, and communities grew in Babylonia, Egypt, and elsewhere. The papyri from Elephantine, a garrison island on the Nile, show a Jewish community there in the fifth century with its own temple to Yahu (the LORD), and a letter of 407 BC in which they asked the governor of Judah, Bagohi, and the sons of Sanballat of Samaria for help to rebuild it after local priests destroyed it. The scattering of Jews outside the land, called the Diaspora (Greek for ‘scattering’), would shape the whole New Testament world.

In 332 BC Alexander the Great marched down the coast after taking Tyre and conquered Gaza and Egypt. Judea passed under his rule, apparently without fighting. When he died in 323 his generals fought over his empire for twenty years. After the battle of Ipsus in 301, Judea belonged to Ptolemy I, who ruled Egypt from Alexandria, and it remained under his dynasty for a century. The Seleucids, the dynasty descended from another general, Seleucus, ruled Syria and Mesopotamia from Antioch and contested Judea in a series of wars. Daniel 11 describes these struggles between ‘the king of the South’ (the Ptolemies) and ‘the king of the North’ (the Seleucids) with a detail that matches the known history closely.

Ptolemaic rule was mostly quiet for the Jews. The high priest governed Jerusalem and was responsible for its taxes, and powerful families bid for the right to collect them. Papyri from the archive of Zenon, an agent of the Ptolemaic finance minister who toured Palestine around 259 BC, mention a local magnate named Tobias, probably of the same family as Nehemiah's opponent Tobiah (Nehemiah 2:10); Josephus tells of his son Joseph, who won the tax-farming contract for the whole region (Antiquities 12.154-236).

The most important legacy of this century was the Septuagint. A large Jewish community grew in Alexandria, and its members spoke Greek. Beginning with the Torah in the third century BC, the Hebrew Scriptures were translated into Greek over the next two centuries. A legendary account, the Letter of Aristeas, says that seventy-two elders translated the Law for the library of Ptolemy II Philadelphus (285 to 246 BC), and the name Septuagint (‘seventy’, abbreviated LXX) comes from that story. The legend is embroidered, but a third-century date for the Greek Torah is widely accepted. The Septuagint became the Bible of Greek-speaking Jews and later of the early church, and it is the version most often quoted in the New Testament.

sections.h: The Seleucids and the crisis under Antiochus IV
sections.body:
Around 200 BC the Seleucid king Antiochus III (‘the Great’) defeated the Ptolemaic army at Panium, near the springs of the Jordan, and took Judea. The Jews of Jerusalem welcomed him, and Josephus preserves a charter in which Antiochus confirmed their right to live by their ancestral laws, exempted the temple staff from taxes, and helped repair the temple (Antiquities 12.138-144). But Antiochus then collided with Rome, lost the battle of Magnesia, and in the Treaty of Apamea (188) was forced to pay Rome an enormous indemnity. His successors needed money, and the temple in Jerusalem held a great deal of it. 2 Maccabees 3 tells how Seleucus IV sent his minister Heliodorus to seize the temple treasury and how he was driven off by a vision.

Antiochus IV, who took the title Epiphanes (‘God manifest’), became king in 175. That year Jason, the brother of the high priest Onias III, bought the high priesthood from him and received permission to make Jerusalem a Greek city, with a gymnasium below the temple mount where young men of priestly families exercised naked in the Greek manner; some even had their circumcision disguised (1 Maccabees 1:11-15; 2 Maccabees 4:7-17). In 172 a rival, Menelaus, outbid Jason, and Onias III, the last legitimate high priest of the old line, was murdered around 171 (2 Maccabees 4:23-34). When Antiochus invaded Egypt in 169, he plundered the temple on his way home. In 168 a Roman envoy, Popillius Laenas, met him outside Alexandria, drew a circle in the sand around him, and demanded an answer before he stepped out of it (Polybius 29.27); Antiochus withdrew from Egypt. Jerusalem, meanwhile, was torn by fighting between Jason and Menelaus, and Antiochus's forces sacked it and built a fortified citadel, the Akra, garrisoned by troops and Hellenizing Jews.

In 167 Antiochus outlawed the practice of Judaism in Judea. Circumcision, Sabbath-keeping, and possession of the Torah were forbidden on pain of death, and on the fifteenth of Kislev (December 167) an altar to a foreign god, identified with Olympian Zeus, was set up on the altar of burnt offering; ten days later pagan sacrifice began on it (1 Maccabees 1:41-64; 2 Maccabees 6:1-11). This is the ‘abomination of desolation’ of Daniel 11:31 and 1 Maccabees 1:54, a phrase Jesus takes up for a future desecration of the temple (Mark 13:14). Many Jews died rather than obey; 2 Maccabees 6 to 7 tells of the old scribe Eleazar and of a mother and her seven sons martyred for refusing pork, who die confessing their hope of resurrection, and Hebrews 11:35 likely alludes to them.

Why a Hellenistic king, whose empire generally tolerated local religions, persecuted this one is still debated. Elias Bickerman (Der Gott der Makkabäer, 1937) argued that the persecution was driven by radical Hellenizing Jews in Jerusalem who wanted to reform Judaism into a universal religion. Victor Tcherikover (Hellenistic Civilization and the Jews, 1959) argued instead that the decrees answered a popular Jewish revolt already under way against Antiochus and his high priest. Others stress Antiochus's need for money and loyalty after his humiliation in Egypt. The biblical and Maccabean writers see in it a test of faithfulness: “the people who know their God will firmly resist him” (Daniel 11:32).

The revolt began in the village of Modein, northwest of Jerusalem, when a royal officer ordered the elderly priest Mattathias to offer a pagan sacrifice. Mattathias refused, killed a Jew who stepped forward to comply and the king's officer with him, and fled to the hills with his five sons, John, Simon, Judas, Eleazar, and Jonathan (1 Maccabees 2). He was joined by the Hasideans (‘the pious’), a group devoted to the Law. When some of the faithful let themselves be slaughtered rather than fight on the Sabbath, Mattathias and his followers decided they would defend themselves even on the Sabbath (1 Maccabees 2:29-41).

After Mattathias died, his third son Judas, called Maccabeus (usually explained as ‘the hammer’), led the fighters. Using guerrilla tactics in the hill country, he defeated a series of Seleucid armies, and in December 164, three years after the desecration, he retook the temple, pulled down the defiled altar, built a new one, and rededicated the sanctuary on the twenty-fifth of Kislev with eight days of celebration (1 Maccabees 4:36-59). The festival of Hanukkah (‘dedication’) remembers that day; John records that Jesus was in the temple at “the Feast of Dedication” (John 10:22). Antiochus IV died on campaign in Persia the same year.

The war went on for two more decades, now as much for political independence as for religious freedom, and it was helped by quarrels within the Seleucid royal family. Judas made a treaty with Rome (1 Maccabees 8), and was killed in battle at Elasa in 160. His brother Jonathan took over, and in 152 a claimant to the Seleucid throne, Alexander Balas, appointed him high priest (1 Maccabees 10:18-21). The family was priestly but not of the line of Zadok that had held the office for centuries, and some Jews never accepted their high priesthood; many scholars think the Qumran community's hostility to the ‘Wicked Priest’ in Jerusalem began here. Jonathan was treacherously captured and killed in 143 or 142. The last brother, Simon, won full independence: 1 Maccabees marks 142 as the year the gentile yoke was lifted from Israel, when documents began to be dated by Simon's years (1 Maccabees 13:41-42). In 140 an assembly of the people made Simon high priest, military commander, and ruler, with the telling proviso that this should hold until a trustworthy prophet arose (1 Maccabees 14:41). He was murdered by his son-in-law in 134.

Simon's descendants, called the Hasmoneans after an ancestor named Hasmon, ruled an independent Jewish state for nearly eighty years. Simon's son John Hyrcanus I (134 to 104) expanded it by conquest. He conquered Idumea (the old Edom, south of Judea) and compelled its people to be circumcised and follow Jewish law, which is how the Idumean family of Herod came to be Jewish. He conquered Samaria and destroyed the temple on Mount Gerizim; coins found there place the destruction around 111 or 110 BC. Josephus reports that Hyrcanus broke with the Pharisees after one of them suggested he give up the high priesthood (Antiquities 13.288-298), and turned to the Sadducees.

His son Aristobulus I (104 to 103) was, according to Josephus, the first of the family to call himself king. He conquered the Itureans to the north, and he is usually credited with bringing Galilee under Jewish rule, which is why Galilee was Jewish territory in Jesus' day. Alexander Jannaeus (103 to 76) spent most of his reign at war, conquering much of the coast and land east of the Jordan, and faced a civil war in which his Jewish opponents, led at least in part by Pharisees, called in a Seleucid army against him. After his victory Josephus says he had eight hundred of his opponents crucified in Jerusalem while he feasted with his concubines (Antiquities 13.380). His widow Salome Alexandra (76 to 67) ruled after him, with her son Hyrcanus II as high priest, and reversed his policy: the Pharisees became powerful in her government.

Her death led to civil war between her sons, Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II. Both appealed to Rome, whose general Pompey was then reorganizing the East. In 63 BC Pompey besieged the temple, took it after three months, and walked into the Most Holy Place, though he did not plunder it. Judea became a tributary of Rome, lost most of its conquests, and was left with Hyrcanus as high priest. The Psalms of Solomon, a collection written soon afterward, lament Pompey's sacrilege and the Hasmoneans' sins and pray for a son of David to come and purge Jerusalem of gentiles and sinners (Psalms of Solomon 17), one of the clearest pictures of messianic hope before the New Testament.

sections.body:
Under Roman oversight the real power in Judea passed to Antipater, an Idumean adviser of Hyrcanus II. He backed Julius Caesar during the Roman civil war, and in 47 BC Caesar rewarded him with Roman citizenship and made his sons Phasael and Herod governors of Jerusalem and Galilee. The Roman general Crassus had meanwhile plundered the temple treasury in 54 on his way to a disastrous war with Parthia. Antipater was poisoned in 43. In 40 the Parthians invaded Syria and Judea and made Aristobulus II's son Antigonus king and high priest; Phasael died in captivity, and Herod escaped to Rome, where the Senate named him king of Judea. With Roman help he took Jerusalem in 37, had Antigonus executed, and began his thirty-three-year reign.

The guide to the Herods and the Roman governors in this series takes up the story from there. By the time of Jesus' birth near the end of Herod's reign, the pieces of the New Testament world were in place: a Roman overlord, an Idumean king, a high priesthood appointed by rulers, a magnificent temple under construction, Greek and Aramaic in the streets, Pharisees and Sadducees, and a people who had fought for their faith within living memory and prayed for God to act again.

sections.h: The writings of the period and the Apocrypha
sections.body:
These centuries produced a large body of Jewish literature. Some books were written in Hebrew or Aramaic, others in Greek. Tobit and Judith are edifying stories set in the Assyrian and Babylonian periods. The Wisdom of Ben Sira (Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus) was written in Hebrew in Jerusalem around 180 BC by a sage named Jesus son of Sirach and translated into Greek by his grandson, who says in his prologue that he came to Egypt in the thirty-eighth year of King Euergetes (132 BC). The Wisdom of Solomon, written in Greek probably in Alexandria, reflects on wisdom, immortality, and idolatry. 1 Maccabees is a sober history of the revolt, probably written in Hebrew around 100 BC; 2 Maccabees, an abridgment of a longer Greek history by one Jason of Cyrene, is more rhetorical and theological, with a strong interest in martyrdom, prayer for the dead, and resurrection. Baruch, the Letter of Jeremiah, and Greek additions to Esther and Daniel complete the collection found in Catholic Bibles; Orthodox Bibles include a few more, such as 1 Esdras, the Prayer of Manasseh, and 3 Maccabees.

Other writings never entered any church's Bible except locally. The book of 1 Enoch, a collection of visions whose oldest parts go back to the third century BC, is quoted in the Letter of Jude (Jude 1:14-15) and remains Scripture in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church. Jubilees retells Genesis and Exodus. The Psalms of Solomon respond to Pompey's conquest. These are usually grouped together as the Pseudepigrapha, ‘falsely ascribed writings’, since many claim the name of an ancient figure. And the Dead Sea Scrolls, from about 900 manuscripts found in eleven caves near Qumran between 1947 and 1956, include both the oldest copies of the Hebrew Scriptures and the rule books, hymns, and biblical commentaries of a sectarian community, most likely Essenes, who lived there from the second or first century BC until AD 68.

Christians disagree about the status of the deuterocanonical books. The Septuagint manuscripts the early church used contained them, and many church fathers quoted them as Scripture; Jerome, translating the Latin Vulgate around AD 400, questioned those not found in the Hebrew Bible but translated some of them anyway. The Catholic Church defined them as canonical at the Council of Trent in 1546, and the Orthodox churches also receive them, with some variation. The Reformers, following the Hebrew canon, placed them in a separate section or left them out: the Church of England's Thirty-Nine Articles (Article VI) says they are read for example of life and instruction in manners but not used to establish doctrine, and Luther's Bible printed them between the testaments as useful and good to read. Whatever their status, no reader can fully understand the New Testament's world without them. The guide to how the books were chosen in this series treats the question more fully.

sections.h: What the period gave the New Testament
sections.body:
Nearly every feature of the Jewish world in the Gospels took shape in these centuries. The synagogue, a local assembly for reading and teaching the Law and for prayer, appears clearly in the Diaspora by the third century BC and in the land by the first. The Jewish parties grew out of the struggles of the Maccabean and Hasmonean periods: Sadducees close to the temple aristocracy, Pharisees devoted to careful observance of the Law and its traditions, and Essenes who withdrew in protest against the Jerusalem priesthood. The guide to the Jewish groups in this series describes each of them. Hanukkah joined the festival calendar. Greek became the common language of the eastern Mediterranean, the Septuagint put the Scriptures into it, and so the New Testament could be written in Greek and read from Rome to Antioch.

Hope changed too. The book of Daniel's promise that “many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt” (Daniel 12:2), and the martyrs of 2 Maccabees, who died expecting God to raise them, made resurrection a widely held Jewish hope; in Jesus' day the Pharisees affirmed it and the Sadducees denied it. The experience of persecution and foreign rule sharpened expectation of God's kingdom and of a Messiah, and the hopes took different shapes: a son of David, a priestly messiah, a heavenly Son of Man, a prophet like Moses. The Gospels show crowds, disciples, and opponents arguing over which of these Jesus was.

The apostle Paul summed up the Christian reading of these centuries in a single line: “But when the time had fully come, God sent His Son, born of a woman, born under the law” (Galatians 4:4). The four hundred years were not an empty gap but the preparation of a people, a language, a hope, and a road system for what was to come.
